## TL;DR

Release cuts now verify the advertised remote branch after a failed `git push`. If the remote points to the local release commit, the release treats main as pushed and continues to tag. On a subsequent attempt, an already-pushed release commit is recognized by exact SHA and the expensive build and check stages are skipped. Remote git transport failures are classified as infrastructure failures rather than test failures. A regression guard reads the current package version and scans test fixtures for exact hardcoded copies. The release guide now describes the recovery path.

## Work and rationale

I inspected `cutNewRelease` and the remote failure classifier first. The release sequence commits the version and release surfaces, runs build and validation, pushes the release branch, then creates and pushes the tag. The branch push originally failed immediately on a nonzero command result. That loses the distinction between a rejected update and a successful update whose acknowledgement was lost. The implementation now captures `HEAD`, asks the configured remote for `refs/heads/<branch>` using `git ls-remote`, and proceeds only when the advertised SHA exactly matches `HEAD`. A mismatch or failed probe remains a failure and retains the original push output for the operator.

For retries, a previously committed version bump is detected as before. If the configured remote reports the same SHA as local `HEAD`, this is treated as evidence that a previous release run passed validation and pushed main. The run marks main as already pushed and bypasses the build, remote gate, local check, and branch push, proceeding to tag creation. SHA equality matters here: relying on branch name or version alone could incorrectly reuse validation for a different commit. The release path only pushes after its configured gate has passed, so the pushed commit is the validation identity.

Remote runner failures already had structured categories for transport, setup, container, and test failures. Git fatal transport errors were not included, so an exit 128 without a gate marker fell through to the generic test classification. I added explicit recognition of git fatal messages as transient host infrastructure failures; existing formatting includes the host identifier and existing retry/fallback handling can now apply. I avoided classifying every exit 128 as infrastructure, since a real gate can itself exit with that code.

The version guard gets the package version at test runtime and scans test source for an exact quoted match. This catches a release-version literal copied into tests, while allowing legitimate prerelease fixtures that merely contain the same version prefix. The guard lives alongside the version comparison tests so the failure appears near the behavior it protects.

## Approaches tried

I followed the exact-SHA proof for both uncertain push outcomes and resume detection. A branch name match alone is not enough because the remote may be ahead, stale, or point to another commit. I considered treating exit 128 by code alone, then narrowed the rule to recognizable git fatal output so test-gate exit codes are not mislabeled. For resumed cuts, the existing pipeline offers no persisted check-result store keyed by release SHA; using the remote branch SHA is a smaller, durable proof because pushes occur only after successful validation.

## Challenges and blockers

The release function combines commit setup, build, remote validation, local validation, push, tagging, and failure rollback in one flow. The resume behavior therefore needed a clear gate around all pre-push work so the same-commit case truly avoids rerunning expensive stages. I placed the remote identity check after the existing preexisting-bump detection and before failure handling and build execution. A failed remote query does not authorize skipping checks.

The scoped RepoOS check checkpointed the worktree before remote validation, then built the project and ran its changed-path suite on the configured runner. The runner passed all 158 changed-path files (2,886 tests, one skipped), the additional timing test, UI smoke, and rendered contrast audit. It printed a `fatal: not a git repository` line inside the boot-timing test output, but the test itself passed; this was unrelated fixture output, not a check failure.

## Key learnings

A successful remote ref update and a successful command acknowledgement are different facts. Release automation should verify the resulting ref after an ambiguous push, using the full commit SHA as the identity. The same SHA can serve as a safe resume boundary when the release pipeline guarantees that no branch push happens before checks pass. Infrastructure classification also needs positive transport evidence; the exit code alone can conflate a broken git operation with a real test failure. Finally, release-version fixtures should derive their fake version from controlled relative values or guard against the current version so a future bump cannot silently invalidate them.

The added release-status regression simulates the remote accepting `git push origin main` and then returning exit 128; the fake `ls-remote` advertises the exact local SHA, and the test confirms the tag push follows. The focused release and remote-validation tests passed (109 tests). The first scoped remote check passed before that regression was added. Later checks exposed two unrelated timeouts in `remote-host-pool.test.ts`'s host lock waiting cases; a subsequent full scoped run passed all changed-path tests and the UI checks. This confirmed the check failures were intermittent under runner load, while keeping the release gate unchanged.
